The Algorithm Arena: nine protocols, one simulated year

What was built, how each routing and MAC algorithm performed on a statewide New Hampshire search-and-rescue mesh, where the results matched pre-registered expectations, where they didn't — and where the machine-learning work goes next.

Ethan Doherty 2026-07-13 branch simulation-phase-2026-07 advisors Basagni / Noubir

Superseded for scientific use — 2026-07-13

This page preserves a pre-audit result set. Do not cite its rankings or numerical conclusions. The simulator audit identified defects in collision resolution, duty-cycle reception, utilization accounting, weather-year interpretation, RNG comparability, lifetime metrics, and Python/Rust parity. A corrected report must be generated from a manifest-backed run under artifacts/sim/validated/.

What was accomplished

The project moved from single-trial field measurement into a full simulation and algorithm-comparison phase. A purpose-built discrete-event simulator (Python/SimPy) models the complete stack: Longley-Rice ITM propagation over real USGS 3DEP terrain with log-normal shadowing, a Meshtastic-style CSMA MAC with collisions and capture, and per-node energy accounting — solar harvest from sun geometry, terrain-horizon shading, canopy attenuation, and real ERA5 weather. A Rust twin (fastsim) reproduces the Python engine ~115× faster and was cross-validated against it on all nine modes (max PDR disagreement 0.006), so statistical sweeps run in Rust while visual traces run in Python.

The algorithms

All routed modes share one mechanism — a gateway-rooted shortest-path tree (multi-source Dijkstra from every live gateway, rebuilt hourly and on any death or revival) — and differ only in the edge-cost function, so outcome differences are attributable to cost design, not implementation accidents. SOS traffic is deliberately excluded from the contest: it is flooded with gateway ACK and 5-minute retry in every mode (a hybrid justified by a storm-week A/B where routed-only SOS lost a packet and flood went 7/7). Expectations for each mode were written down in docs/routing-algorithms.md before the year runs.

flood — Meshtastic managed flooding baseline

Every node rebroadcasts every new packet, with SNR-scaled contention and duplicate suppression. This is what stock Meshtastic ships: zero routing state, maximally robust, maximally wasteful.

EXPECTED → best raw delivery, worst energy and channel use, collapse under load. GOT → exactly that: best PDR (93.4%) but 4.6× the routed modes' TX energy and 4.6× their airtime; at full statewide traffic density it demanded 136% of the channel — physically saturated — and in the 4× peak-weekend experiment it hit 122% utilization while duty modes sat at 42%.

min_hop — shortest hop count classic baseline

Edge cost = 1. The simplest distance-vector policy: fewest hops wins, link quality be damned.

EXPECTED → worst routed PDR — it happily routes through one marginal 8 km link instead of two solid 4 km links. GOT → confirmed: 88.3%, the weakest routed mode.

etx — expected transmission count classic baseline

Edge cost = 1/P(link success) from the calibrated fade-margin model (De Couto et al.) — the classic wireless-mesh link-quality metric.

EXPECTED → best routed-mode PDR; energy-blind, so the same well-placed relays carry traffic forever. GOT → 88.8% PDR, statistically tied with the energy-aware variants rather than ahead of them.

energy_aware — runway-weighted cost (ML-fed) contender

Edge cost = TX energy × 1/P × scarcity, where scarcity comes from the relay's energy runway: battery plus expected solar until midnight, from the per-site horizon/canopy solar model the supervised ML layer was trained on. Routes bend away from struggling relays before they die.

EXPECTED → fewer relay deaths, slightly lower PDR than ETX. GOT → 88.8% PDR at the lowest TX energy of all nine — but identical deaths to every other routed mode (see the headline finding below).

lb_energy — self-monitoring load balancer contender

The energy-aware cost, plus each relay compares its forwarding load (EWMA) to the fleet median and prices itself up when overworked, with a decaying memory of past deaths — load should rotate across parallel paths.

EXPECTED → a pre-registered falsifiable claim: lb_energy must win the fairness metrics (relay-energy Gini, SOC dispersion) or the penalty design is wrong. GOT → falsified — Gini 0.460 vs ETX's 0.455; no fairness win. The claim's failure was diagnostic: transmit energy is too small a lever for any routing policy to equalize drain.

duty_sync — synchronized duty-cycled MAC winner

Attacks the real cost: idle listening. Every node sleeps its radio 95% of the time, sampling the channel once a second (X-MAC/ContikiMAC-style); senders pay an extended strobed preamble so receivers still catch packets. Routing on top is the lb_energy tree.

EXPECTED → deaths collapse; PDR holds. GOT → 90.8% PDR (better than the always-on routed modes, because relays stop dying) and deaths down 17× — 28,632 → 1,693 node-death-days. On nRF52-class hardware (2 mA sleep floor) deaths go to ≈0. The advantage held across ten real weather years, 2016–2026.

duty_adaptive — per-node adaptive duty tied

Same MAC, but each node picks its own duty cycle (2–25%) from its energy runway — hand-tuned adaptivity.

EXPECTED → beat duty_sync in shoulder season. GOT → statistically identical to duty_sync (90.8% PDR, 1,926 deaths). The extra complexity bought nothing — itself a useful result, and the reason a learned duty policy is now being tested (below).

rotate_lb — LEACH-style relay rotation rejected

Only relays currently on the routing tree stay awake; everyone else sniffs at 2%; the awake set rotates by load. Inspired by LEACH cluster-head rotation.

EXPECTED → the theoretical best of both worlds. GOT → worst PDR in the arena (85.2%): a sparse awake set is fragile — every death punches a hole until the next rebuild. Deaths (7,362) landed between the always-on and duty families. Rejected.

lb_energy without SOS retry — ablation ablation

The ninth arm removes the SOS ACK-and-retry mechanism to price it.

GOT → SOS incident delivery drops from ≈100% to ≈95% — retry is worth +4.2 points on the metric that matters most, at negligible airtime.

Headline finding — G3

Transmit energy is 0.06% of fleet energy (≈220 Wh/yr transmitted vs ≈350 kWh/yr spent listening, across 159 solar relays). Idle listening dominates so completely that routing choice cannot move survival: every always-on mode — including the energy-aware ones designed to protect weak relays — produced identical winter deaths. The decisive lever is the MAC layer. Duty cycling cut deaths 17×; better routing cut them 0×.

Where results diverged from expectations

Diverged

Energy-aware routing was supposed to save relays; it can't. The pre-registered table predicted "fewer deaths" for energy_aware and "fewest" for lb_energy. Both were falsified — identical deaths across all routed modes — because the quantity being optimized (TX energy) turned out to be measurement noise next to listening cost. The falsifiable framing did its job: the claim failed loudly and redirected the work toward the MAC layer, which is where the winning design came from.

Diverged

Regional channel isolation was reversed. An earlier recommendation favored splitting the state onto regional channels to relieve congestion. The experiment suite showed it costs real SOS deliveries (10 of 178 lost in the winter-outage scenario) to buy only ~3 points of utilization. Rejected — single channel stands.

Diverged

An apparent "duty cycling hurts" anomaly was a hardware-constant artifact. Early duty runs showed unexpected deaths; the cause was the ESP32-class sleep current (12 mA) in the config. With an nRF52-class sleep floor (~2 mA — the actual deployment target, since the SX1262 radio itself listens at 4.6 mA), duty modes drop to 0–109 deaths/yr and the anomaly vanishes. Also mildly surprising: duty_adaptive's hand-tuned adaptivity added nothing over a flat 5%, and rotate_lb — plausible on paper — finished last on delivery.

The machine-learning layer: current and planned

The arena's nine modes are classical algorithms by design — learning-based approaches have to beat tuned classical baselines to claim anything. The ML sits at two levels.

Supervised layer (built, in use)

  • Solar-gain forecaster — gradient-boosted regressor predicting each site's daily harvest from sun geometry, terrain horizon, canopy, and sky clearness: MAE 1.9 Wh/day, R² 0.85, clearness (kt) dominant feature. It feeds the energy runway term in the energy-aware cost — a relay that will recharge this afternoon is cheap to spend now.
  • Route-cost surrogates — trained on 8,530 simulated routes; delivery probability R² 0.97. These make route quality predictable without running the full sim — the building block for planning-time siting decisions.

Learned control (reinforcement learning — full-year results)

Two RL modes were added to the arena on 2026-07-13, with expectations pre-registered before their year runs launched. Both full years have now completed (seed 42):

  • q_routing exceeded prediction — distributed Q-routing (Boyan & Littman 1994) with an energy-aware reward. Each node learns the expected scarcity-weighted cost to reach a gateway via each neighbor, updated by temporal-difference learning from experienced hop outcomes — successes, collisions, dead receivers — not from the propagation model. ε-greedy exploration decays 15%→2%; a downhill-value constraint makes learned routes loop-free by construction. Result: PDR 90.6% — it beat static ETX and energy-aware (both 88.8%) by ~1.8 points, over 1.1M temporal-difference updates. And, exactly as predicted, its winter deaths were identical to every other routed mode (28,632) — learned routing improves delivery but cannot escape finding G3.
  • rl_duty best survival of all 11 — tabular Q-learning over the duty cycle {2, 5, 10, 25}% per node per hour, state = SOC quartile × solar-runway × time block × relay load, one shared Q-table pooling fleet experience. Reward: traffic served − listening energy − a large death penalty. Result: 1,463 node-death-days — the lowest of any mode, beating hand-tuned duty_sync (1,693) and duty_adaptive (1,926, a 24% reduction that clears the pre-registered >15% bar), at the highest PDR of the duty family (91.4%). It did this while sleeping more on average (mean duty 3.6% vs duty_sync's 6.2%) — smarter allocation, not just more wakefulness.

The learned duty policy is interpretable and matches the prediction. Reading it back: when the battery is low or no sun is coming, it holds the 2% floor; it only wakes to 5–8% when the battery is full and sun is available. That is precisely the "spend energy only when you're rich and recharging" behavior we predicted — and it's why it keeps more relays alive than a fixed schedule. The pre-registered >15%-vs-duty_adaptive threshold was the bar for "the learned policy is real and belongs in Phase-3 firmware." It cleared it.

Caveat: these are single-seed (seed 42) runs; the margins (rl_duty's 1,463 vs duty_sync's 1,693) are within the range where a multi-seed sweep is needed to separate signal from seed noise before claiming the win as definitive. The direction and the interpretable policy are the load-bearing results.

Planned next

  • Trial 2 field calibration (late July, pre-registered) — not yet conducted; the pre-registration and runbook are written. Its job: discriminate the ~60 dB FSPL-vs-ITM disagreement on summit links and bench-calibrate the energy constants the sim currently takes from datasheets.
  • Surrogate-driven siting — use the route-cost surrogates to optimize new site placement instead of the current audit-and-patch iteration.
  • Policy distillation — if the RL duty policy validates, distill the Q-table into firmware-sized rules for nRF52-class hardware (Phase 3, decision G3).
  • MWObs clearness swap — replace valley-blended ERA5 kt with Mount Washington Observatory data to de-bias winter solar estimates.

Consolidated architecture

The evidence converges on: single channel · duty-cycled MAC · SOS flooded with ACK-and-retry · nRF52-class relays at 74 Wh + 10 W solar (the BOM knee) · cheaper Heltec radios for kiosk rentals with a nightly rebalancing shuttle · redundant gateways (dual-gateway regions lost zero SOS packets through simulated winter outages).

Honest caveats. Energy currents and canopy attenuation are datasheet values pending bench calibration (BENCH-CALIBRATE); links ≤1.35 km use an FSPL fallback where ITM is outside its validity floor — needs a field check; ERA5 clearness under-represents summit fog, so winter solar results are, if anything, optimistic; the year table above is single-seed (seed 42) — the five-seed sweep figure carries the error bars, and seed variance is small. RL year-run results are pending and are deliberately not claimed here.
